openingProblem.problem: Brezhnev ruled for eighteen years without a famine, a purge or a sudden reversal of policy, and most Soviet families acquired a television and a refrigerator. Yet his successors called his rule an 'era of stagnation'. Was it stability or decline?

chunks.title: Collective leadership and economic reform, 1964–1970
chunks.body:
In October 1964 Khrushchev's colleagues removed him. Power passed to a collective leadership in which **Leonid Brezhnev** led the party and **Aleksei Kosygin** headed the government.

In 1965 Kosygin launched an ambitious **economic reform**. Enterprises would now be judged by goods sold rather than goods produced, would pay interest on their capital and could reinvest their profits. The aim was a more flexible economy able to satisfy consumers. But the reform was undermined from the start. Managers still could not set prices, so they relied on unofficial fixers, the *tolkachi*. Workers saw tighter discipline as a breach of the unwritten social contract: "they pretend to pay us, and we pretend to work". Demand that the official economy could not meet turned to the illegal **second economy**, which the economist Gregory Grossman later named and which Vladimir Treml estimated at 10–12 per cent of GDP.

The new leaders did keep some of Khrushchev's social gains: his pension scheme was extended to collective farmers after 1965. And living standards rose. Between 1965 and 1980 refrigerators reached 86 per cent of urban families, televisions 85 per cent and washing machines 70 per cent, while car ownership more than tripled.

This mattered because reform was abandoned rather than deepened, which meant that rising consumption came to depend on the illegal economy rather than on a more efficient system.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The Kosygin reform aimed at flexibility.
The second economy filled the gaps.

useItInAnEssay.claim: The Kosygin reform failed because it changed incentives without changing the system.
useItInAnEssay.prove: From 1965 enterprises were judged by goods sold and could reinvest profits, but managers still could not set prices and turned to unofficial fixers.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that the central planners kept control of the most important economic signal, so enterprises could not respond to demand.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, living standards still rose, with refrigerators reaching 86 per cent of urban families by 1980.
useItInAnEssay.judge: The reform therefore failed as a reform, even though consumption grew without it.

chunks.title: The Brezhnev Doctrine and the end of reform hopes, 1965–1968
chunks.body:
Brezhnev's leadership quickly tightened control over ideas. In September 1965 the writers Andrei **Sinyavsky** and Yuli **Daniel** were arrested for publishing fiction abroad. Sentenced in February 1966 to seven and five years in labour camps, they were, Judt notes, the first people imprisoned solely for the content of their writing. Their trial produced protests inside the Soviet Union, and the **dissident movement** and *samizdat* (self-publishing) date from that moment.

The decisive test came in Czechoslovakia, which Brezhnev had long regarded as the least reliable member of the Warsaw Pact. In January 1968 **Alexander Dubček** became party leader and launched "socialism with a human face": cultural freedom, economic reform and limits on the secret police. The Soviet Politburo was alarmed, especially as many Soviet intellectuals hoped the "Prague Spring" would spread. On **21 August 1968** Warsaw Pact troops invaded, and Dubček was removed in April 1969. The **Brezhnev Doctrine** asserted the right of fraternal communist parties to intervene against "antisocialist degeneration": each party, Brezhnev said, was "not free to deviate" from Marxist-Leninist principles.

Judt sees August 1968 as the definitive turning point: the illusion that communism could be reformed "was crushed under the tanks on August 21st 1968 and it never recovered". At home, he concludes, the regime settled in "for an indefinite twilight of economic stagnation and moral decay".

This mattered because Brezhnev's leadership chose control over reform both at home and in the bloc, which meant that change could no longer be expected from within the ruling party.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The Sinyavsky–Daniel trial marked a crackdown.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: It also created the dissident movement.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The Brezhnev Doctrine limited the bloc's sovereignty.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: It was unpersuasive even to western communists.

argumentsThatWork.claim: August 1968 ended hopes of reform from above.

howItGetsAsked: Evaluate the significance of the Brezhnev Doctrine for the Soviet Union and its allies between 1968 and 1982.
To what extent was the Brezhnev era a period of stagnation between 1964 and 1982?

useItInAnEssay.claim: The invasion of Czechoslovakia ended the hope that communism could reform itself.
useItInAnEssay.prove: Warsaw Pact troops entered Prague on 21 August 1968, and the Brezhnev Doctrine claimed the right to intervene against 'antisocialist degeneration'.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that any communist party that reformed too far would be overruled by force, so, as Judt argues, reformers stopped looking to the party.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the invasion also damaged the Soviet Union's reputation, and even western communists condemned it.
useItInAnEssay.judge: August 1968 was therefore a victory for control that cost the regime its claim to reform.

chunks.title: Détente, dissent and Afghanistan, 1969–1980
chunks.body:
In foreign policy Brezhnev sought recognition. From the late 1960s to the mid-1970s **détente** eased tensions with the West. The **SALT I** treaty of 1972 limited strategic arms, and the **Helsinki Accords** of 1975 recognised Europe's post-war borders, a major Soviet aim. For Moscow, détente meant formal acceptance of military parity with the United States.

But Helsinki also contained human-rights promises. Soviet citizens formed groups to monitor compliance, and the regime decimated them with arrests: their founder Iurii Orlov was arrested in February 1977 and sentenced to seven years' hard labour. Dissidents never numbered more than a few thousand, but they had moral weight. The *Chronicle of Current Events* recorded abuses from 1968; Solzhenitsyn was deported in 1974. On 22 January 1980 **Andrei Sakharov**, father of the Soviet hydrogen bomb and a Nobel Peace Prize winner, was exiled to Gorky after protesting against the war in Afghanistan. The regime now preferred decrees to show trials, but by 1980 the dissident movement was in ruins.

Détente did not survive Brezhnev's decline. In **December 1979** the Soviet Union invaded Afghanistan to restore a compliant regime on its southern border. The United States led a boycott of the 1980 Moscow Olympics, and détente was over.

This mattered because Brezhnev achieved recognition of Soviet power abroad while repressing those who invoked the same agreements at home, which meant that détente exposed the contradiction between the regime's image and its practice.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Détente brought recognition of Soviet power.

howItGetsAsked: Compare and contrast the domestic and foreign policies of Brezhnev between 1964 and 1982.
Evaluate the significance of the Brezhnev Doctrine for the Soviet Union and its allies between 1968 and 1982.

useItInAnEssay.claim: Détente brought the Soviet Union recognition but also exposed it to criticism at home.
useItInAnEssay.prove: The Helsinki Accords of 1975 recognised Europe's post-war borders, a major Soviet aim, but their human-rights provisions inspired monitoring groups that the regime decimated with arrests.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that détente gave dissidents an international standard to appeal to, so repression became more embarrassing for the regime.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, by 1980, with Orlov imprisoned and Sakharov exiled, the dissident movement was in ruins.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Détente therefore strengthened the regime abroad while creating a new kind of challenge at home.

chunks.title: Stagnation or stability? The 'Little Deal'
chunks.body:
How should the Brezhnev years be judged? The word **stagnation** (*zastoi*) was coined only in the late 1980s, as part of Gorbachev's case for reform; at the time, the official term was "developed socialism", declared at the Twenty-Fourth Party Congress in 1971. For many citizens, the early 1970s felt like an era of quiet improvement: better-stocked shops, private flats instead of communal ones, and less demand for ideological fervour.

The economist James Millar called the arrangement the "**Little Deal**": the regime offered rising incomes, secure jobs, more consumption and tolerance of petty dealing on the side, in return for political quiet. The Ninth Five-Year Plan (1971–75) promised a 42 per cent rise in retail sales. But the deal rested on an economy that could not deliver quality, and on the illegal second economy to fill its gaps. The educated white-collar class, which grew from 3.3 to 21.4 million between 1950 and 1974, became quietly disillusioned.

At the top, the leadership aged. Brezhnev accumulated titles, marshal in 1976 and head of state in 1977, promulgated a new Constitution in 1977, and even received the Lenin Prize for literature, while his health and that of the ageing Politburo declined and corruption spread. Prestige projects such as the **Baikal-Amur Mainline**, revived in 1974, served no clear economic purpose. Brezhnev died in 1982.

This mattered because the regime bought stability with consumption and tolerance of corruption rather than with reform, which meant that historians can call the same years both a time of stability and the beginning of decline.

useItInAnEssay.claim: The Brezhnev era was stable on the surface and stagnant underneath.
useItInAnEssay.prove: Under the 'Little Deal' incomes and consumption rose, with televisions in 85 per cent of urban families by 1980, while the second economy supplied what the plan could not.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that citizens accepted political quiet in exchange for comfort, so the regime faced little open protest.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the term 'stagnation' was coined only in the late 1980s, and many citizens remember the early 1970s as an era of quiet improvement.
useItInAnEssay.judge: The era was therefore one of stability bought at the cost of the reforms the economy needed.

segments.text: Brezhnev's domestic and foreign policies shared one aim: stability.
At home the 'Little Deal' traded consumption for quiet, whereas abroad détente produced SALT I in 1972 and the Helsinki Accords of 1975, recognising post-war borders.
This meant that in both spheres the regime sought acceptance of the status quo, so it crushed challenges, from Czechoslovakia in 1968 to Sakharov in 1980.
However, abroad Brezhnev won formal gains, while at home stability came without reform, and the invasion of Afghanistan in 1979 ended détente.
His policies were therefore alike in aim and method, but more successful abroad until 1979 than at home.

essayQuestions.text: Analyse the methods used by the Soviet regime to deal with dissent between 1965 and 1982.

decodeKey.verb: Analyse: break the question into its parts and show how they connect
decodeKey.judgement: Which method mattered most, and how they connect

modelPlan.thesis: The regime dealt with dissent through trials, labour camps and exile, deportation abroad, administrative decrees and propaganda, preferring methods with a veneer of legality to Stalin's terror.
modelPlan.counter: Most Soviet citizens were not dissidents, which made repression easier.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which mattered most? Exile and imprisonment of leaders, which left the movement in ruins by 1980.

segments.text: The regime defeated dissent by isolating its leaders rather than by mass terror.
Sinyavsky and Daniel were sentenced in 1966, Solzhenitsyn was deported in 1974, Orlov was imprisoned in 1977 and Sakharov exiled to Gorky by decree in 1980.
This meant that dissent was punished with an appearance of legality, so by 1980 the dissident movement was in ruins.
However, the 'Little Deal' mattered as much: by offering comfort in exchange for quiet, the regime kept most citizens from joining dissidents.
Repression of leaders and the 'Little Deal' therefore worked together to contain dissent.
